scope.start: 13b: the broken-vessels baraita, brought against the view that a Jew acquires from a gentile with money (opens mid-exchange)
scope.end: 14b: Rava's answer from the school of R. Yishmael, leaving Devarim 17:1 for R. Elazar's private altar

sections.title: Money or Meshikhah from a Gentile? Four Readings of the Broken-Vessels Baraita
sections.gist: Continuing the question of how a Jew acquires from a gentile, the Gemara tests it on a baraita about an idol found among scrap metal, read four ways: through Jewish law with Abaye's *mekach ta'ut* (mistaken purchase) or Rava's appearance, Rav Ashi's money alone, and Ravina's reneging on a verbal commitment.

bullets.text: The upshot matters in practice: selling *chametz* before Pesach, selling land for *shemittah* and selling an animal to a gentile to avoid *bekhor* all depend on which act transfers ownership to a gentile.

Rashi follows the thrust of this sugya, that a gentile acquires with money. Most Rishonim follow Ameimar, who holds that *meshikhah* acquires. So the accepted practice is to do both: the gentile pays and also takes possession.

A further device is to rent the gentile the place where the *chametz* or the animal stands. Everyone agrees a gentile acquires land with money, and whatever stands on his land is in his possession. Whether *chalipin* (symbolic barter) also works is debated.

children.title: The Baraita: Pulled Before Paying or After, and a Jewish-Law Stipulation
children.gist: A buyer who pulled before paying may return the idol, but one who paid first may not; the Gemara explains this through a sale the gentile agreed to put under Jewish law.

bullets.text: Baraita: one who buys broken gold or silver vessels from gentiles and finds an idol among them. If he pulled before paying, he may return it. If he pulled after paying, he may not, and must cast it into the Dead Sea.
The Gemara brings this as an objection to the view that one acquires from a gentile with money: if money acquires, why does pulling (*meshikhah*) matter?
Answer: the gentile accepted that the sale be judged by Jewish law, under which *meshikhah* acquires.
Then why mention money at all? The baraita means that even after he paid, everything depends on the pulling: if he pulled, he acquired; if not, he did not.
On its face the baraita seems to require both money and *meshikhah*, which fits neither the money view nor the *meshikhah* view.

children.title: Pulled Yet Returnable: *Mekach ta'ut* or Appearance of a Jew's Idol?
children.gist: If *meshikhah* acquires, why may the buyer in the first clause give the idol back? Abaye calls it a *mekach ta'ut*, Rava points to how it looks, and Abaye answers Rava's objection with the buyer's duty to inspect.

children.title: Abaye's Mekach Ta'ut vs. Rava's Appearance
children.gist: Abaye: the first clause is a *mekach ta'ut*. Rava: the latter clause is just as mistaken; the real difference is that once money was paid, the idol looks like it belongs to the Jew.

bullets.text: Difficulty: the first clause says he pulled before paying and may still return it, so pulling alone seems not to acquire.
Abaye: the first clause is a mistaken purchase (*mekach ta'ut*), since the Jew never meant to buy an idol.
Rava objects: then the latter clause is a *mekach ta'ut* too. In neither case did he want the idol.

Rava: both clauses are mistaken purchases. Where he hadn't paid the dinars, it doesn't look as if a Jew owns an idol, so he may return it. Where he had paid, it looks as if a Jew owns an idol, so he must cast it away.
For Rava *meshikhah* is what acquires in both clauses. Money decides only whether giving the idol back would look like a Jew selling an idol.
Even unpaid, an onlooker sees the idol handed back. But the Sages set a general rule for the case most likely to mislead: before payment, people assume he simply withdrew.

children.title: Abaye's Rejoinder: Once He Paid, He Should Have Inspected
children.gist: Abaye can keep his distinction: a buyer who has already paid should inspect before pulling, so his error doesn't void the sale.

bullets.text: Abaye: the first clause is a *mekach ta'ut* because, not having paid, he had not yet inspected the goods.
In the latter clause, having paid, he should have inspected before pulling. He didn't bother, so the sale stands.

Tosafot: normally payment doesn't create a duty to inspect that cancels a mistaken-purchase claim. Buying from a gentile is different, since the buyer should expect idolatrous items among the goods. That risk is already close to defeating the claim, and the payment tips it over.

children.title: Rav Ashi: Gentile Law, Money Alone Acquires
children.gist: Rav Ashi reads the baraita under gentile law, where only money acquires; the latter clause says "pulled" only because the first clause did.

bullets.text: Rav Ashi: the sale is under gentile law, and only money acquires.

As for the difficulty raised against R. Oshaya's view (why mention pulling?): pulling acquires in neither clause. The first clause said "pulled" to show it is ineffective, and the latter clause repeated the word though it isn't needed.
This is the simplest reading and fits the sugya's working assumption that money acquires from a gentile.

children.title: Ravina: Meshikhah in Both Clauses, and Reneging Without Bad Faith
children.gist: Ravina reads both clauses under Jewish law: in the first the buyer neither paid nor pulled, and "returns" means he backs out of his word, which is not *mechusar amanah* with a gentile.

bullets.text: Ravina: the sale is under Jewish law. Since *meshikhah* acquires in the latter clause, it acquires in the first clause too.
The first clause means he neither paid nor pulled, and "returns" means he reneges on his verbal commitment: he need not complete the purchase.
The *tanna* had to say this because he holds that backing out of a verbal commitment is an act of bad faith (*mechusar amanah*).
That applies between Jews, who are assumed to keep their word. Between a Jew and a gentile, where neither side is assumed to rely on the other's word, reneging is not bad faith.
This reflects the circumstances of the Talmudic period and the fraught relations with surrounding non-Jewish society. It shouldn't be read as a timeless statement about interpersonal ethics.

sections.title: Mishnah: Blemish Before Consecration vs. Consecration Before Blemish
sections.gist: An animal blemished before it was consecrated holds only a *kedushat damim* (sanctity of value) and is fully freed by redemption; one consecrated first holds *kedushat ha'guf* (inherent sanctity) that lingers after redemption. *Bekhor* and *ma'aser* follow the second pattern even when blemished first.

bullets.text: This Mishnah also appears in Hullin and is treated at length in Temurah.

children.title: Blemish First: Only Its Value Is Sacred, Fully Freed by Redemption
children.gist: A permanently blemished animal that was then consecrated holds only a *kedushat damim*; once redeemed it is ordinary in every respect, except for a *bekhor* or *ma'aser*.

bullets.text: A permanent blemish before consecration: the animal has no *kedushat ha'guf*, only its value is sacred.

Once redeemed, its offspring can be counted a *bekhor*, the priestly gifts (foreleg, jaw and maw) are given, it becomes fully non-sacred, and it may be shorn and worked. Its offspring and milk are permitted after redemption.
Slaughtering it outside the Temple courtyard carries no *karet*. It does not make a *temurah* (substitute) consecrated. If it died before redemption, it is redeemed and fed to dogs, not buried.
Exception: a *bekhor* and *ma'aser behemah* have *kedushat ha'guf* even when blemished before they became sacred, like offerings that were consecrated and then blemished.
This *kedushat damim* is directed to the altar: the proceeds must buy an offering. That sets it apart from a plain *bedek ha'bayit* dedication for Temple upkeep.

Why *bekhor* and *ma'aser* differ: their sanctity comes from birth and from being counted tenth, not from a person's declaration, so a prior blemish can't limit it. Of the tithe the Torah says "whether good or bad."
It can be redeemed after death because neither obstacle applies: it needs no standing before the priest, and redeeming it doesn't count as redeeming an offering to feed dogs.

children.title: Consecration First: *Kedushat ha'guf* That Outlasts Redemption
children.gist: An animal consecrated before its permanent blemish (even with a temporary one earlier) keeps restrictions after redemption, and carries the full consequences of an offering.

bullets.text: Consecration before the blemish, or a temporary blemish before consecration and a permanent one after: once redeemed, its offspring are not counted a *bekhor* and no priestly gifts are given.
It never becomes fully non-sacred for shearing and labor. Its offspring conceived before redemption, and its milk, remain forbidden after redemption.
Slaughtering it outside the courtyard carries *karet*, it makes a *temurah* consecrated, and if it died before redemption it is not redeemed for dogs but buried.
These are *pesulei ha'mukdashin*, to whom the Sages apply "you may slaughter, but not shear; eat, but not work" (*tizbach ve'lo gizah, ve'akhalta ve'lo avodah*).
The *karet* for slaughter outside applies only to a blemish slight enough that the animal would stay on the altar once brought up, such as a cataract. *Temurah* works only before redemption.

sections.title: Gemara on the First Case: Bekhor, Shearing, Offspring, Slaughter Outside
sections.gist: The Gemara works through the first case clause by clause: *kedushat damim* exempts from *bekhor*; the shearing ban doesn't prove R. Eliezer; offspring conceived before redemption and redeemed without a blemish, contrasted with Rava's rule; and R. Elazar's reading of slaughter outside as a *bamat yachid* (private altar).
sections.continues: Continues at 14b.14 with the Mishnah's clauses on *temurah* and on animals that died before redemption: R. Shimon, the Rabbis and the school of Levi on standing and valuation.

children.title: Kedushat Damim Exempts from Bekhor and Priestly Gifts
children.gist: The obligations start only once the animal is redeemed, so even a *kedushat damim* exempts from *bekhor* and the gifts while it lasts.

bullets.text: The Mishnah ties *bekhor* and the gifts to redemption. So before redemption the animal is exempt.
The *tanna* holds that *kedushat damim*, a sanctity of value alone, exempts from *bekhor* and the priestly gifts.
The exemption doesn't need altar sanctity; any sanctity will do. Compare a donkey dedicated to the Temple treasury: its foal is not subject to *peter chamor*.

children.title: Shearing Before Redemption: Proof for R. Eliezer on Bedek Ha'bayit? No
children.gist: The ban on shearing an unredeemed blemished animal seems to support R. Eliezer's ban for *bedek ha'bayit* animals, but the Gemara limits it to value sanctity for the altar, which can be confused with *kedushat ha'guf*.

bullets.text: The Mishnah frees the animal for shearing and labor only once redeemed. So before redemption both are forbidden.
This seems to support R. Eliezer, who forbids shearing and labor with animals dedicated to *bedek ha'bayit*, since both hold only a *kedushat damim*.

Rejected: an animal whose value is sacred for the altar can be confused with an altar animal of *kedushat ha'guf*, so the Sages decreed against shearing and labor. For *bedek ha'bayit* animals there is no such concern and no decree.

The owner tried to make it an offering, and only the blemish reduced it to a *kedushat damim*, whose proceeds still buy an offering. It sits between altar sanctity and a plain Temple-upkeep dedication, which is why it is easily confused with a real offering.

children.title: Offspring of a Blemished Consecrated Animal: When Conceived, and Must They Wait for a Blemish?
children.gist: Three steps on the offspring: which case the Mishnah means, whether such offspring are redeemed unblemished, and how a direct consecration of an unblemished male differs.

children.title: Conceived Before Redemption, Born After
children.gist: The Mishnah's permitted offspring must be conceived while the mother was consecrated and born after she was redeemed; if born before, they stay forbidden until redeemed.

bullets.text: If conceived and born after redemption, it is obvious that the offspring are permitted: they were never sacred.
So the Mishnah means conceived before redemption and born after: they are permitted although conceived while the mother was consecrated.
Inference: if born before redemption, the offspring are forbidden until they are redeemed.
Redeeming the mother removes the sanctity from the fetus along with her.

children.title: Redeemed Without a Blemish? The Subsidiary Is Not Stricter than the Primary
children.gist: A baraita rules that the offspring of permanently blemished animals dedicated for the altar may be sold without waiting for a blemish, since the offspring can't be holier than the mother.

bullets.text: Background: the offspring of an animal with *kedushat ha'guf* is born sacred and can't be redeemed until it is blemished.
Question: may the offspring of an animal whose value alone is sacred be redeemed unblemished, or must one wait for a blemish?
Baraita: one who dedicates permanently blemished animals for the altar, and they gave birth: the offspring are sold and need no blemish.

Two reasons: sanctity does not take effect on them, and the subsidiary should not be stricter than the primary (*she'lo yehei tafel chamur min ha'ikar*). The mother is redeemed at once, so the offspring are too.
The offspring are themselves unblemished, which makes the question real: they carry a sanctity that could never have led them to the altar.

children.title: Unblemished Male Consecrated for Its Value: *Kedushat ha'guf* (Rava)
children.gist: The offspring escape altar sanctity only because theirs comes through a blemished mother; an unblemished male consecrated directly for its value becomes an offering, as Rava says.

bullets.text: The baraita's only reason is that the subsidiary follows the primary: the offspring's sanctity comes from a mother who can't be sanctified for the altar.
But one who consecrates an unblemished male for its value, with no secondary sanctity involved, gives it *kedushat ha'guf*.
This supports Rava: one who consecrates a male for its value (*hikdish zakhar le'damav*) sanctifies it with *kedushat ha'guf*.

Rashi: this applies to value sanctity aimed at buying an offering. If the animal is fit, it is itself the offering, so there is no reason to take the long way round. A dedication purely for Temple upkeep would not become *kedushat ha'guf*.

children.title: Slaughtered Outside: R. Elazar's "Liable" and the *bamat yachid*
children.gist: R. Elazar reads the Mishnah as "liable" for offering on a *bamat yachid*, from Devarim 17:1, and the Gemara defends that use of the verse against four other candidates.

children.title: R. Elazar: Devarim 17:1 Forbids a Blemished Animal on a Bamat Yachid
children.gist: R. Elazar's version of the Mishnah says "liable": lashes for offering a blemished animal on a *bamat yachid*, since the public altar's rule already has its own verse.

bullets.text: R. Elazar teaches the Mishnah as "one who slaughters them outside is liable," referring to a private altar (*bamat yachid*).
The liability is not *karet* for slaughter outside the courtyard, but lashes for offering a blemished animal on a *bamat yachid*.

Source: "You shall not sacrifice to the Lord an ox or a sheep in which is a blemish" (Devarim 17:1). The public altar is already covered by "blind or broken" (Vayikra 22:22), so apply this verse to a *bamat yachid*, at a time when private altars are permitted.

children.title: Why Not Firstborn, Tithe, *temurah* or Offspring? Each Has Its Own Source
children.gist: Four animals sacred despite a blemish are proposed as the verse's subject; each is already forbidden elsewhere, so Devarim 17:1 stays with the *bamat yachid*.

bullets.text: Challenge: apply the verse to a *bekhor*. It is sanctified even when permanently blemished, so one might think it can be offered blemished.
Answer: the *bekhor* has an explicit verse: "if there be any blemish therein, lameness or blindness… you shall not sacrifice it" (Devarim 15:21).
Challenge: apply it to *ma'aser behemah*, which is sacred even blemished ("he shall not inquire whether it be good or bad," Vayikra 27:33).
Answer: a *gezerah shavah* from "passing," said of both the tithe and the firstborn. As a blemished firstborn is not offered, neither is a blemished tithe animal.
Challenge: apply it to a substitute (*temurah*), which becomes sacred even when blemished ("a good for a bad," Vayikra 27:10).
Answer: "it and that for which it is substituted shall be holy" compares the *temurah* to the original. As the original is not offered blemished, neither is the *temurah*.
R. Zeira: apply it to the offspring of offerings, sacred even when blemished because of their mother.

Rava: the school of R. Yishmael already derived it from "Only your sacred items which you have, and your vows" (Devarim 12:26). "Sacred items" are substitutes, "which you have" are offspring, and "your vows" puts them on a par with a vowed offering, which is not offered blemished.
So Devarim 17:1 refers to a *bamat yachid*, as R. Elazar holds.
The unifying point: whether an animal is sacred and whether it can be offered are two separate questions. A blemish may not stop the sanctity, but it always bars the altar.

key_terms.definition: An act of acquisition in which the buyer pulls or draws a movable object into his possession. By rabbinic enactment it is the standard way of acquiring movables between Jews.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The broken-vessels baraita is read with *meshikhah* acquiring under a Jewish-law stipulation (Abaye, Rava, Ravina) or as irrelevant under gentile law (Rav Ashi).

key_terms.definition: A transaction made under a material mistake, such as an undisclosed defect, which the wronged party may cancel.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Abaye explains why the buyer may return the idol as a mistaken purchase, and limits it to a buyer who had not yet paid and so had no duty to inspect; Rava holds both clauses are mistaken purchases.

key_terms.sense: bad faith in reneging on one's word
key_terms.definition: The moral failing of backing out of a verbal commitment to a transaction, even where no binding act of acquisition was performed.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Ravina's *tanna* holds reneging is bad faith between Jews, who rely on each other's word, but not in a sale with a gentile.

key_terms.sense: sanctity of an animal's value only
key_terms.definition: Consecration that attaches to an item's monetary worth rather than to the item itself, so it is redeemed or sold and its value goes to the sanctuary.
key_terms.on_this_daf: An animal blemished before consecration holds only this sanctity: it still exempts from *bekhor* and the gifts before redemption, forbids shearing by rabbinic decree, and its offspring may be redeemed unblemished.

key_terms.definition: Consecration of the animal itself as an offering for the altar, which cannot be removed by redemption unless the animal becomes blemished, and even then leaves lasting restrictions.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Animals consecrated before their blemish, and a *bekhor* or *ma'aser* even if blemished first, have it; Rava holds an unblemished male consecrated for its value acquires it too.

key_terms.sense: substituting an animal for an offering
key_terms.definition: Declaring an ordinary animal a replacement for a consecrated one. The Torah forbids it, but the substitute becomes sacred alongside the original.
key_terms.on_this_daf: A substitute takes effect for an animal consecrated before its blemish but not for one blemished first; a blemished substitute cannot be offered, since the verse compares it to the original.

key_terms.definition: An individual's altar outside the central sanctuary, permitted during certain periods of Israel's history before the Temple was built.
key_terms.on_this_daf: R. Elazar reads the Mishnah's slaughter outside as offering a blemished animal on a private altar, forbidden by Devarim 17:1.

judgment_calls: The four readings of the baraita (13b) are grouped under one top-level section because they all answer the same objection. Abaye and Rava are nested together under 'Pulled Yet Returnable' since they share one question about the first clause. Rav Ashi and Ravina could have been nested with them as parallel readings; they sit alongside instead because each rereads the whole baraita.

The shiur's practical summary (chametz, shemittah, bekhor; doing both money and meshikhah) has no Gemara lines of its own, so it is attached as shiur bullets to the parent section s1 rather than made a separate section.

The Gemara on the Mishnah's first case (14a.5–14b.13) is one top-level section with a child for each clause it examines. The private-altar derivation is long enough to be its own top-level section, but it is the Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's 'slaughtered outside' clause, so it is kept in that series.

Rava's rule on an unblemished male consecrated for its value (14b.3) could be a separate section on sanctity upgrades. It is kept under the offspring discussion because the Gemara derives it by contrast with the baraita on offspring.
The four challenges to R. Elazar's verse are one section with a chart rather than four children, since each is a single challenge and answer.
coverage_notes: The essay calls the broken-vessels source a mishna in Avodah Zarah; the text calls it a baraita. Followed the text.

The segmentation attributes the Jewish-law stipulation answer to Abaye; in the text it is the Gemara's anonymous answer, and Abaye's contribution is the mistaken-purchase explanation. Followed the text.
The essay says the buyer who paid must cast the idol's monetary value into the Dead Sea; the text says he casts the idol itself. Followed the text.
The essay attributes the view that bedek ha'bayit animals are forbidden in shearing and labor to R. Elazar; the text (14a.6) has R. Eliezer. Followed the text.

The essay attributes the private-altar reading to R. Eliezer and describes the majority as disagreeing; the text has R. Elazar, who teaches the Mishnah as 'liable' and refers it to a private altar, and the Gemara ends by upholding that reading. Followed the text.
The essay attributes the offspring challenge to Rav Zevid; the text has R. Zeira, answered by Rava citing the school of R. Yishmael. Followed the text.

The essay's halachic summary is internally confused about the Rishonim's reasoning; the outline keeps only its clear claims (Rashi follows money; most Rishonim follow Ameimar's meshikhah; practice is both), consistent with the previous daf's essay.
The donkey and peter chamor example, Tosafot on the duty to inspect, Rashi's limit on Rava, and the cataract and temurah qualifications are the lecturer's additions and are marked as shiur.
14b.14 onward (the temurah derivation, animals that died before redemption, R. Shimon, the Rabbis and the school of Levi) falls outside this outline's scope; the shiur does not reach it.
